newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Amnesty urges respect for rights in Cameroon poll.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges respect for rights in Cameroon poll.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International on Monday called for human rights to be respected in the run-up to Cameroon's parliamentary elections.
The opposition, which has not agreed a common platform for Saturday's poll, has complained of harassment and says its supporters have experienced problems registering to vote.

In a statement faxed to news agencies, the London-based group called on the government of President Paul Biya to allow all citizens to vote without fear of arrest, detention or ill-treatment and said human rights violations continue.
"We are seriously concerned that further human rights violations may occur during the parliamentary elections," Amnesty said.
Saturday's elections will be the second parliamentary poll since a return to multi-party politics in 1990.

Amnesty said an estimated 200 people, and possibly more, remained in detention since a security sweep of Cameroon's North-West province following a series of armed attacks on security forces in the opposition heartland in March.
Amnesty said most of those arrested belonged to the opposition Social Democratic Front (SDF) and many were tortured and ill-treated during their detention.
The English-speaking North-West province is a flashpoint in the largely French-speaking Central African country.
SDF ChairmanJohn Fru Ndi, a bitter rival of Biya, demanded that a curfew in the region, imposed after the violence, be lifted if elections were to be fair.

"If the elections should proceed with the curfew still in place, instructions shall be issued to our militants to remain in the polling stations beyond the curfew hour in order to defend their vote until counting," Fru Ndi said in a protest letter.

Gilbert Andze Tsoungui, deputy prime minister in charge of territorial administration, announced last week that the curfew had been relaxed and would run from 9.30 p.m. to 6 a.m. instead of 7 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The SDF complains that supporters have not been registered, while foreigners from neighbouring Nigeria, Chad and the Central African Republic are being given voting cards to bolster support for Biya's ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Rally (RDPC) party.
A scuffle between supporters of the two parties broke out in the capital Yaounde on Monday in which one SDF supporter's leg was broken.

"We shall storm their offices on May 14 for a sit-in if we are not given the cards, if they want let them kill us," said Njakwa Leoline, an SDF coordinator in the port city of Douala, where the SDF won January municipal elections.

Many opposition parties boycotted the last parliamentary poll in 1992, leaving the RDPC with 88 out of 180 seats in the national assembly. It formed an alliance with the small Movement for the Defence of the Republic (MDR) to ensure a majority.
This time 45 parties will field 1,800 candidates to contest the seats.

Political analysts say the number of opposition parties taking part, and the lack of any effective alliance, may leave the way clear for the ruling party to win the 91 seats it needs to govern without looking for support from other parties.
"We are prepared this time around to work extra hard to avoid the headache of begging for alliances," said ruling party secretary general Charles Doumba.
Cameroon is an exporter of crude oil as well as agricultural produce including coffee and cocoa.
